title: KV cache — defragmentation playbook & observability
body:
Purpose
This is a pragmatic operational playbook and design note focused on reducing KV cache fragmentation, making compaction safe to run in production, and adding observability to make fragmentation actionable. Not a full allocator spec — complements the allocator proposals (slab & slabless) by focusing on: metrics, detection thresholds, incremental/controlled compaction strategies, runtime scheduling, and rollout plan.

Background / problem statement
- Our inference workloads have highly skewed KV size distributions: small prefixes (hundreds of bytes) mixed with long LH sequences (KB+). Over time this produces internal fragmentation in the KV heap when we use variable-sized chunk allocation.
- Fragmentation manifests as: rising resident memory without proportional token throughput, increased OOM incidents on tail events, and higher latency spikes due to GC/compaction pauses.
- Current mitigations (aggressive eviction, simple free-lists) are blunt: they drop useful cached context, increase model recompute cost, and don't reclaim scattered free space efficiently.

Goals (what success looks like)
1) Reduce useful memory overhead caused by fragmentation by >=25% on heavy mixed workloads (measured as fragmentation_ratio; see metrics below).
2) Keep compaction pauses per node <10ms on p95 for normal traffic; allow safe emergency compaction with controlled latency impact for critical low-memory conditions.
3) Make fragmentation visible in dashboards and tie alerts to automated policies (eg. start background compaction when fragmentation_ratio > 0.3 AND free_memory < 20%).
4) Provide an incremental rollout path: feature flagged, canary to 5% of serving fleet, and easy rollback.

Key concepts & definitions
- chunk: allocation unit returned by allocator (variable size).
- fragment: free chunk or small non-contiguous free region that can't satisfy incoming allocation without splitting/merging.
- fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (largest_contiguous_free / total_free) [0..1]; higher => worse.
- slack window: short-lived reservation window at allocation time that allows coalescing adjacent frees before release to global free-list (helps reduce transient fragmentation).

Observability (instrumentation plan)
Metrics to add (per-node, per-arena):
- kv_total_bytes (gauge)
- kv_used_bytes (gauge)
- kv_free_bytes (gauge)
- kv_largest_contiguous_free_bytes (gauge)
- kv_fragmentation_ratio (derived) = 1 - largest_contiguous_free / kv_free_bytes
- kv_alloc_request_size_pXX (histogram)
- kv_compaction_runs_total (counter)
- kv_compaction_time_ms_p50/p95 (histogram)
- kv_compaction_written_bytes_total (counter)
- kv_pinned_bytes (gauge) (amount currently pinned by long-lived requests)
- kv_evictions_total (counter), kv_eviction_reasons (label)
- kv_async_scan_backlog (gauge) (number of arena pages pending scan for compaction)
Alert rules (examples):
- P0: fragmentation_ratio > 0.5 AND free_bytes < 0.15 * total_bytes for 2m -> page SRE and start emergency compaction job (see safety below)
- P1: fragmentation_ratio > 0.3 for 5m -> slack-background-compaction on low-priority lane

Design: hybrid background compaction model
We propose a two-tier defragmentation system that balances low-latency serving with long-running compaction work:
1) fast path: thread-local arenas + slack-window coalescing at free time
   - Allocations go to thread-local arenas to reduce contention and spatially group similar-sized chunks.
   - On free, a short slack-window (configurable 2–50ms) defers immediate return to the global arena; if an allocation arrives that can reuse during the window, we avoid creating isolated free fragments.
   - Slack-window is opt-in per arena; defaults off for nodes with very tight memory SLOs.
2) background incremental compactor (low priority, cooperative)
   - Scans arenas for fragmentation hotspots (fraction of small scattered free chunks vs larger contiguous regions).
   - Uses incremental copy-compact: pick an under-utilized page/segment, migrate live chunks out to new contiguous pages, update references and free old pages.
   - Add per-migration rate limits (bytes/sec) and time-slice per-runtime tick to keep p99 latency unaffected.
   - Compactor runs on a separate cgroup/worker pool with tunable niceness; we expose throttle controls via runtime flags and Console.
3) emergency compaction (higher risk)
   - Triggered by the P0 alert or when free memory < threshold for N seconds.
   - Evicts non-pinned cold entries aggressively to free contiguous blocks, then performs targeted compaction on the hottest arenas.
   - Emergency compaction is allowed to take short pauses on request threads (bounded and measured) but should prefer preemption-friendly techniques first.

Allocator interactions & layout recommendations
- Keep page/segment granularity at 64KB or 256KB (experiment required). Larger page sizes reduce metadata overhead and improve contiguous free space but can increase internal slack.
- Maintain two complementary free-lists: small-chunk segregated lists (+ size classes) and page-level free-list for whole-page reuse.
- When performing incremental compaction, prefer copying small, high-reuse entries to minimize write amplification.
- Reservation & pinning: long-context requests (eg. RLHF or stream restore) can pin KV ranges. The allocator must expose pin APIs with timeouts; compactor must not move pinned ranges but may schedule aggressive eviction for pinned-but-stale entries.

Scheduling & runtime integration
- Compaction jobs run in background worker pool separate from inference lanes. Integrate with serving runtime scheduler so jobs back off when inference queue depth or latency increases.
- Expose backpressure signal: compactor should subscribe to a circuit-breaker (latency SLO metric) and reduce work rate if SLOs degrade.
- Integrate with rollout/fallback: if compactor causes regressions during canary, automatically toggle to lower intensity or rollback via feature flag.

Safety, correctness & pointer updates
- Copy-compact requires safe pointer updates for live KV references across threads. We must: mark moved items under a short muting window, update references atomically, and support rollback if migration fails.
- Consider a small CAS-based indirection table for KV entries: compaction updates a single pointer rather than touching many caller caches. Tradeoff: indirection cost vs. compaction simplicity.

Operational playbook (runbooks)
- Daily dashboard: fragmentation_ratio by fleet, compaction_throughput, compaction_pause_p95.
- Runbook for P1 (moderate fragmentation): enable slack-window on top-affected arenas for 6h, start low-intensity background compactor on affected nodes.
- Runbook for P0 (severe fragmentation): initiate emergency compaction, drain non-critical traffic from nodes, evict cold caches, escalate to SRE.
- Canary checklist: correctness tests (no stale pointer reads), latency SLOs (p50/p95), memory-reservation smoke tests, GPU memory behavior (if KV resides in GPU staging).

Experiments & measurement plan (short term)
1) Synthetic workload: mixed small/large KV sizes with 80/20 hot-key distribution. Baseline fragmentation ratio with current allocator.
2) Run slack-window enabled vs disabled at 10% canary for 24–48h; measure change in fragmentation_ratio and latency.
3) Evaluate incremental compactor with different page sizes (64KB/256KB/1MB). Measure compaction throughput and pause distribution.
4) Validate pointer-atomicity approach using stress tests with concurrent reads/writes and network failover.

Tradeoffs and known unknowns
- Indirection vs direct pointers: indirection simplifies compaction but adds per-access overhead. We need perf microbenchmarks to quantify.
- Slack-window effectiveness varies by workload; for bursty traffic it helps, for steady-state may add allocation latency.
- Compaction I/O and memory bandwidth will compete with inference kernels on shared nodes — need hard limits.

Implementation roadmap (phases)
- Phase 0 (spike, 2w): build fragmentation metrics + dashboard; small alloc instrumentation.
- Phase 1 (prototype, 6w): implement thread-local arenas + slack-window; run internal experiments.
- Phase 2 (compactor, 8w): incremental compactor worker, safety primitives (pin API, migration atomic update), ops runbook drafted.
- Phase 3 (canary & rollback, 4w): roll out to 5% with intensive monitoring; iterate on throttle heuristics.
- Phase 4 (fleet rollout, 6–8w): gradual ramp, trainings, SRE runbook finalization.

Open decisions (need design meetings)
- Acceptable page/segment sizes for us (64K vs 256K) — schedule perf benchmark.
- Indirection table adoption? perf budget for extra memory accesses.
- Slack-window default duration and per-arena opt-in policy.

TODOs (short-term)
- [ ] Create dashboard panel prototypes (Noah)
- [ ] Add metrics hooks to current allocator (Ethan)
- [ ] Write simulation harness for mixed-size KV workloads (Maya)
- [ ] Draft JIRA tickets for compactor worker and pin API (owner: Maya)

Notes to reviewers
- This doc is intentionally ops-focused: it assumes allocator-level primitives exist (free, reserve, pin, page-level move) and lists how to orchestrate compaction safely and observably. Please call out missing allocator APIs we need or safety concerns around pointer consistency.

References
- See linked artifacts for Confluence dashboard drafts and the early PR with allocator metrics.
- Related discussions: slack thread TS05K2H4J; earlier proposals around slabless designs (some overlap).
